newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish bond yields to remain low after auction.
newsitem.headline: Turkish bond yields to remain low after auction.

text.p: Turkish Treasury bill and bond yields are likely to remain low following a week-long downward trend and the Treasury's first ever 399-day bond issue at sharply lower yields on Tuesday, bankers said.

"The market is a bit cautious after the 10-day strong drop. But sellers in the market are weak, so there is demand for new issues despite interest rates currently running low," said the securities manager of a private bank.

In line with previous expectations the Treasury sold a record 373.3 trillion lira of 399-day bonds at 112.42 percent, including 12 percent witholding tax, down sharply from 125.45 percent in the previous 392-day bond auction on December 24.
The previous record was 311.1 trillion lira of one-year bonds sold in an auction on October 25.
Following a plunge of around 20 percentage points across the board in the last 10 days, all T-bill and bond yields stood below 100 percent for the first time in more than a year.
The downtrend began last Monday after a government move to raise witholding tax on interest income from state securities to 12 percent from 10 on papers to be issued this year.
A cabinet decision to delay the introduction of income tax on interest income from bonds and bills by one year to 1999 also boosted public and bank demand for outstanding state securities.

Bankers said rising liquidity since last week, lower than expected December inflation data and the central bank's rate cuts in its money market limits on Monday prompted further sharp falls in bond market yields.

"Monday's sharp drop was in reaction to inflation data and the central bank's rate cuts. Current low levels indicate a monthly inflation expectation of 5.5 percent, but it is too early to predict inflation in 1997," a private banker said.

Consumer prices rose 3.4 percent in December against a 5.2 percent rise in November, the State Institute of Statistics said over the weekend. It said wholesale prices increased 3.9 percent last month, after a 5.1 percent jump the previous month.

In a long-awaited move, the central bank on Monday lowered its overnight money bid-offer rates by one point to 56-77 percent, cut its t/n offer rate to 72 percent from 74 and its tomorrow/week bid-offer rates by two points to 63-73 percent.

Bankers also noted that economic policies, central bank operations, new inflation-indexed plus premium borrowing instruments expected to be launched soon and overnight money rates would affect the downtrend in the medium and long-term.
"The treasury still needs heavy borrowing and the banks have to earn money from bond trading," a private bank treasurer said.

The Treasury will collect 159.7 trillion lira from banks for today's auction on Wednesday when it will meet 162.6 trillion lira of T-bill maturities. Its domestic debt servicing will be around 1,000 trillion lira in the first quarter of 1997.
Bankers say the Treasury is trying to extend its domestic borrowing maturities to above one year in an effort to meet the government's 1997 budget targets.
The zero-deficit 1997 budget envisages domestic debt servicing to be cut to 29.8 percent of total expenditures from 38.2 in 1996. The 1996 deficit is seen at 1,300 trillion lira.

T-bill and bond portfolios of Turkish banks nearly tripled to 686.7 trillion lira on December 6, from 258.4 trillion at the end of 1995. Many bankers warn that banks carrying large bond portfolios are at risk in case of a sudden rise in bond yields.
Turkish banks made good profits from T-bill and bond portfolios and trade in 1996 due to high real interest rates of up to 40 percent. Last year's inflation was around 80 percent.
The newly-issued February 11, 1998 paper traded at 99.45 percent after the auction, compared to 101.66 auction yield, excluding 12 percent witholding tax.
